ecovero.types: LENZING ECOVERO is sold as viscose staple fiber in the usual textile deniers and cut lengths for ring, open-end and air-jet spinning; the brand is defined by sourcing and process documentation rather than by a new chemistry. The main variants Lenzing promotes are standard ECOVERO viscose, ECOVERO black, a spin-dyed (dope-dyed) fiber in which black pigment is added to the dissolved pulp before extrusion so the color runs through the fiber, and ECOVERO made with REFIBRA technology, which adds recycled cotton pulp to the wood pulp. Lenzing presents ECOVERO as a viscose brand, so the generic name on an ECOVERO label should be viscose (rayon in the US).
ecovero.fabrics: ECOVERO goes wherever ordinary viscose goes: fluid challis and crepe for dresses and blouses, printed rayon wovens, viscose jersey for T-shirts and tops, and blends with cotton, polyester, linen or elastane. Spun viscose yarns made from it are used in knitwear and in soft suiting blends. Spin-dyed ECOVERO black targets knits and wovens where deep, wash-stable black is the selling point. Because the fiber is chemically ordinary viscose, the fabric's hand, drape and shrinkage depend on the mill's yarn and finishing, not on the brand.
ecovero.quality: The label must say viscose or rayon; ECOVERO may appear only in addition. Lenzing states that the fiber carries an identification system that lets it detect ECOVERO in finished products long after spinning and dyeing, so brands can ask for verification. Genuine branded hangtags are issued through Lenzing's E-Branding Service against a licensed fabric. For the fabric itself, look for a dense, even weave that does not slip at the seams, since viscose seams fray easily. Ask whether the fabric was preshrunk; rayon wovens can shrink several percent on first wash. Very low prices for 'ECOVERO' fabric sold by the meter without documentation are a red flag.
pros: It keeps the drape, luster and absorbency that make viscose popular while adding documented sourcing.
Lenzing's built-in fiber identification allows the brand to be checked in finished goods, unlike generic viscose.
Lenzing reports an EU Ecolabel license for the fiber, a third-party scheme with published criteria.
The spin-dyed black variant resists fading because the pigment sits inside the fiber rather than on it.
cons: It is still viscose: weak when wet, prone to shrinkage and creasing, and easily distorted by wringing.
The xanthate route still uses carbon disulfide, so the brand improves rather than removes the chemistry concerns of viscose.
Environmental savings are quoted against a generic viscose baseline chosen by the producer.
The brand gives no information on fabric weight, weave density or finishing, which decide durability.
ecovero.impact: Lenzing's headline claims are that ECOVERO production causes about half the emissions and water impact of generic viscose and that the wood comes from FSC or PEFC certified sources; these are producer comparisons against its own definition of generic viscose. For the spin-dyed black version, trade reporting quotes Lenzing as saying that dyeing in the dope can roughly halve water use and cut the dyeing stage's carbon footprint by about 60% compared with conventional dyeing. Independent evidence at the end of life favors cellulose over plastics: a 2019 study by Zambrano and colleagues found rayon microfibers biodegraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester microfibers persisted, although cellulose fabrics shed more microfiber mass in washing. Social and pollution risks in the wider viscose industry (carbon disulfide exposure, effluent) are the reason site-level data matter.
ecovero.care: Wash viscose gently: cold to 30 C, delicate or hand-wash cycle, mild detergent, and a mesh bag for fluid wovens. Do not wring or twist, because wet viscose loses much of its strength; roll in a towel to remove water, then dry flat or on a padded hanger. Tumble drying invites shrinkage and seam distortion. Iron on a medium setting (the two-dot range, about 150 C) on the reverse while slightly damp, or steam, to avoid shine. Store clean and dry to prevent mildew. Dark prints can bleed at first wash, so wash separately. Check the label; many rayon challis garments are safer dry cleaned.
faq: Is ECOVERO better than regular viscose?

It is the same fiber type with different sourcing, process controls and documentation. Performance in wear is essentially that of good viscose. What differs is the producer's reported environmental data, certification and the ability to verify the fiber in finished goods, all of which should be checked for the product.

It can, like any viscose. Shrinkage depends on how the fabric was woven or knitted and whether it was preshrunk or resin finished. Wash cool, avoid the dryer, and expect some relaxation shrinkage on the first wash of untreated fabric.

Viscose is regenerated cellulose and in laboratory tests rayon microfibers biodegrade in aerobic aquatic conditions. Real garments contain dyes, finishes, threads and often synthetic blend fibers, which change the outcome, so biodegradability claims should be read as applying to the fiber under stated test conditions.
notable: ECOVERO black is colored in the spinning dope, so the black pigment is locked inside each fiber rather than dyed onto the surface afterward.
Lenzing says ECOVERO can be detected in a finished garment by its fiber identification system, which it later extended to TENCEL fibers.
